sections.name: Top stories
sections.label: Top stories
sections.glance: Four labs at the top of the independent index, four open-weight releases with the Chinese ones ahead on cost, the agent-containment story becoming a regulated event, decision models as a category, and ARC-AGI-3's harness gap across three labs. Holds the cost against score chart and the harness animation.
sections.lead: Five stories from three weeks. Two are about where the frontier now sits: four labs within five points of each other on the independent index, and an open-weight tier where the newest American entry, Meta's first open frontier-scale weights, came in below the Chinese models on both score and cost per task (the chart under the second story puts every new model on one plane). Then the follow-up to last issue's sandbox escape, which became a story about every service an agent is allowed to reach; the arrival of decision models as a product category; and ARC-AGI-3, where the same models score about 50% or about 97% depending on which harness runs them (the animation replays it model by model).

sections.name: Models & releases
sections.label: Models
sections.glance: Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 as the ChatGPT default, Argon and Muse details, Mistral Large 4, DeepSeek 1017, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Grok Voice 3.0, Nemotron 3.5, MAI-Base-2 and three smaller open releases.
sections.lead: Every lab with a page in this knowledge base shipped something except Qwen and Kimi. The thread is price per capability at every tier: Anthropic's smallest model fell 90% in price, OpenAI replaced Sol after a week at the same price with a cheaper cache, DeepSeek improved its Flash model without touching the price and added paid search, and the open releases each lead with an efficiency claim (active parameters, bits, tokens per second). Scores are the vendors' unless marked as Artificial Analysis or Vals AI.

sections.name: Research & papers
sections.label: Research
sections.glance: On-policy distillation's controlled study, Context Language Models, the Sharpening Tax, looped models, four-bit RL rollouts, OpenAI's 722 manuscripts, the METR re-fit, hidden capabilities and new agentic benchmarks.
sections.lead: The window's papers keep asking what post-training actually adds. The on-policy distillation study finds the KL direction matters more than who wrote the rollouts; the Sharpening Tax paper finds post-training narrows what agents can solve at pass@K; Context Language Models moves context management from harness code into the model. On the measurement side, OpenAI's mass release of machine-written mathematics met its first withdrawals within a day, and a statistical re-fit of METR's time horizons argues the famous plot's units are not uniform. Three of these papers get their own pages in Papers. Two Anthropic research posts close the tab: how far models are from copying themselves onto cheap hardware, and a cryptographic archaeology result.

sections.name: Industry
sections.label: Industry
sections.glance: Revenue figures that diverge on accounting, financing strain in the debt markets, enterprise rationing of Claude Code, US and Chinese policy, ownership changes.
sections.lead: Money became measurable and contested at the same time. OpenAI's and Anthropic's revenue figures stopped being comparable once it emerged that only one counts cloud-partner sales; the debt markets priced the buildout's risk (a 15.78% yield on CoreWeave paper, a cancelled $5B IPO); and two of the biggest enterprise buyers rationed the most expensive coding agent. Policy moved in both capitals: a voluntary US accord and China's draft controls on exporting large models.

sections.name: Compute & chips
sections.label: Compute
sections.glance: AMD Helios shipping, Maia 300, Micron on 2027 and 2028 supply, GPU rental prices rising, NVIDIA's China share, TSMC's quarter and a 3.59 GW power deal.
sections.lead: Supply, not demand, is the constraint every number here describes. AMD's rack-scale answer to NVIDIA moved from announced to shipping, Microsoft's in-house accelerator reached HBM4, Micron said memory will be tighter in the next two years than in this one, and GPU rental prices rose instead of falling. In China the shift away from NVIDIA showed up in market share.

sections.name: Dev tooling & agents
sections.label: Dev tools
sections.glance: Python 3.15, vLLM v0.32.0 and SGLang v0.5.22, Claude Code's Mods and defaults, OpenCode 2.0 and its breach, Pi 1.0, Copilot sandboxing, the Codex daemon, Anthropic's Scion, PostgreSQL 19 RC 1, Deno to Cloudflare, LiteLLM.
sections.lead: Two kinds of change mattered for anyone running these tools. Releases with breaking defaults: vLLM dropped Python 3.10 and changed what max_tokens means, uv now installs Python 3.15, LiteLLM stopped launching local MCP servers. And the agent tools themselves became infrastructure with infrastructure's problems: a coding agent that leaves a self-updating daemon behind, a hosted console that leaked users' provider keys, and a lab that replaced git because agents now make thirty thousand merges a day.

sections.name: Talk of the town
sections.label: Talk
sections.glance: Containment rather than rogue agents, default budget caps, Karpathy's widening gap, the DeepSeek price argument, what benchmarks miss, and GitHub's outage postmortem.
sections.lead: The arguments of the window, with their Hacker News readings. Most were about control: whether "rogue agent" stories are really containment failures, whether spending limits should be on by default, and whether the gap between what people think models do and what they do is growing. Points and comments were read on 2026-10-19.

glance.label: At a glance
glance.lead: Three weeks in one issue, 2026-09-28 to 2026-10-19: 73 items across models, research, industry, chips, developer tools and the window's arguments, each with its sources. The issue was written from the sources on 2026-10-19; where a claim rests on one outlet or a vendor, its card says so. This tab is the window in one screen; every section has its own tab with the items in full.
glance.theme: The window's theme: the number depends on who measures it and how. The same model scores 50% or 97% on ARC-AGI-3 depending on the harness; the two largest labs' revenue figures differ because only one counts cloud resale; the open-weight leader depends on whether you rank by score or by cost per task; and the agent incidents turned on which "allowed" services counted as the network. Read every figure in this issue with its harness, its reporter and its denominator. The [[cost against score chart|t-top|v-cost]] and the [[harness animation|t-top|v-arc]] make two of these concrete.
